Writing your own model or dataset

George Kachergis

2026-11-12

Source: vignettes/custom-models.Rmd
custom-models.Rmd

Every model in XSLmodels is an xslMod: a learning function plus its parameters. Every dataset is an xslData: training trials, test trials and, optionally, human responses. Anything that follows these two contracts works with xsl_run(), xsl_fit(), cross-validation and the evaluation functions. This vignette builds one of each.

A new model

The learning function

A model function takes three arguments and returns an xslFit:

  • params: a named list of the model’s parameters.
  • data: the training trials, a list of words and objects with one entry per trial. xsl_run() relabels both as positions 1..n in their sorted vocabularies before calling the model, so the model can index its matrix with them directly, and it puts the original labels back afterwards. Missing words or objects on a trial are NA.
  • control: an xslControl(). A model should honour reps (train on the sequence this many times, recording performance after each block) and keep_traj (record the matrix after every trial only when asked), and should use start_matrix if it declares support for it.

It returns xslFit(perf = , matrix = , traj = ), where matrix is the word-by-object matrix of association strengths that test trials are scored on, and perf holds each word’s probability of choosing its referent: one row per training block (get_perf() computes it with Luce choice).

As an example, here is a “rich get richer” learner. On each trial, each word shares one unit of associative weight among the objects present, in proportion to its current association with each, plus a constant eps. Everything decays by C per trial. With a small eps a word quickly commits to the objects it has already been associated with; a large eps spreads the weight evenly, which amounts to counting co-occurrences.

rich_get_richer_model <- function(params, data, control) {
  C <- params[["C"]]
  eps <- params[["eps"]]
  voc <- sort(unique(unlist(data$words)))
  ref <- sort(unique(unlist(data$objects)))
  m <- if (is.null(control$start_matrix)) matrix(0, length(voc), length(ref)) else control$start_matrix
  dimnames(m) <- list(voc, ref)
  perf <- matrix(0, control$reps, length(voc))
  traj <- list()
  for (rep in seq_len(control$reps)) {
    for (t in seq_along(data$words)) {
      w <- stats::na.omit(data$words[[t]])
      o <- stats::na.omit(data$objects[[t]])
      m <- m * C
      if (length(w) && length(o)) {
        share <- m[w, o, drop = FALSE] + eps
        m[w, o] <- m[w, o] + share / rowSums(share)
      }
      if (isTRUE(control$keep_traj)) traj[[length(traj) + 1]] <- m
    }
    perf[rep, ] <- get_perf(m)
  }
  xslFit(perf = perf, matrix = m, traj = traj)
}

The constructor

A constructor wraps the function and its parameter values in an xslMod. Set stochastic = TRUE if the model draws random numbers, so that xsl_run() averages control$n_sim simulations, and supports_start_matrix = TRUE only if the function really uses control$start_matrix (otherwise xsl_run() stops rather than silently ignoring one).

rich_get_richer <- function(C, eps) {
  xslMod(name = "rich_get_richer",
         description = "Shares each word's weight in proportion to its current associations",
         model = rich_get_richer_model, params = list(C = C, eps = eps),
         stochastic = FALSE, supports_start_matrix = TRUE)
}

The new model now runs, and is scored, like any other. Here it is on five conditions where what a learner already knows matters: the co-occurrence baseline() fits them badly.

labels <- vapply(xsl_datasets, `[[`, "", "label")
conds <- xsl_datasets[labels %in% c("215", "216", "219", "220", "225")]
run <- xsl_run(rich_get_richer(C = .97, eps = .5), conds)
run$sse
#> [1] 0.6263171
xsl_run(baseline(), conds)$sse
#> [1] 2.189507

Fitting it

xsl_fit() searches the parameters named in free (by default, the leading parameters) within the bounds given, here with two restarts and a seed for reproducibility. A small DEoptim search keeps this vignette quick; use the defaults for a real fit.

fit <- xsl_fit(rich_get_richer(C = .97, eps = .5), conds,
               lower = c(.5, .001), upper = c(1, 10), free = c("C", "eps"),
               n_restarts = 2, seed = 1,
               deoptim_control = DEoptim::DEoptim.control(NP = 20, itermax = 15, trace = FALSE))
fit[[1]]$optim$bestmem
#>         C       eps 
#> 0.9950217 0.2308525
fit[[1]]$optim$bestval
#> [1] 0.2977749
fit[[1]]$restarts
#> [1] 0.2979941 0.2977749
fitted <- update_params(rich_get_richer(C = .97, eps = .5), fit[[1]]$optim$bestmem,
                        free = c("C", "eps"))

Checking it

A few properties are worth checking for any new model. These are the checks tests/testthat/test-invariants.R applies to every model in the package.

  • Output is valid on every condition: associations are finite and accuracies lie in 0,10, 1.
  • Output is valid at the edges of the fitting bounds, where numerical problems tend to hide.
  • Labels don’t matter: relabelling the words and objects shouldn’t change the predictions.
corners <- list(c(.5, .001), c(.5, 10), c(1, .001), c(1, 10))
runs <- lapply(corners, \(p) xsl_run(rich_get_richer(C = p[1], eps = p[2]), xsl_datasets))
all(vapply(runs, \(r) all(vapply(r$fits, \(f) all(is.finite(f$matrix)) &&
                                   all(f$perf >= 0 & f$perf <= 1), TRUE)), TRUE))
#> [1] TRUE

A new dataset

An xslData needs training trials. To compare a model with people, it also needs the tested items and human accuracy.

  • train: a list of words and a list of objects, one entry per trial. Labels can be numbers or strings, and a word’s correct referent is the object with the same label.
  • test (optional): the tested words and, for each test trial, the objects offered. Without a test, each word is tested among all objects.
  • test$correct (optional): when the correct choice isn’t the word’s own object. For example, the filtering conditions test each word with its own object absent, where the correct choice is the object it was paired with.
  • accuracy and n_subj: the proportion correct per test item and the number of participants.
  • response_matrix (optional): for each test item, how many participants chose each object, with one column per object in sorted label order. It supports choice-level likelihoods and choice_probabilities().

Here is a small three-word design with string labels, tested 3AFC. “dax” appears on three trials, the others on two:

my_data <- xslData(
  train = list(words = list(c("dax", "wug"), c("dax", "fep"), c("wug", "fep"), "dax"),
               objects = list(c("dax", "wug"), c("dax", "fep"), c("wug", "fep"), "dax")),
  test = list(words = list("dax", "wug", "fep"),
              objects = list(c("dax", "wug", "fep"), c("dax", "wug", "fep"), c("dax", "wug", "fep"))),
  accuracy = c(.8, .5, .4), n_subj = 10,
  # columns: objects in sorted order (dax, fep, wug)
  response_matrix = rbind(c(8, 1, 1), c(3, 2, 5), c(4, 4, 2)),
  label = "toy", condition = "3 words, 1-2 per trial")
my_data
#> xslData object with label "toy" and condition "3 words, 1-2 per trial"
#>   training trials: 4
#>       test trials: 3
#>             words: 3
#>           objects: 3
#>        accuracies: 3
#>          subjects: 10

xslData() checks that the pieces fit together: one accuracy and one response-matrix row per test item, and one column per object. Each row of the response matrix should also reproduce the item’s accuracy: here, 8 of 10 participants chose dax for “dax”. (Note that 4 of 10 chose fep for “fep”, and fep is the second column.)

The model can be scored against it, at the level of accuracy or of the individual choices:

f <- xsl_run(fitted, my_data)$fits[[1]]
f$perf
#> [1] 0.7543542 0.6300001 0.6299896
ch <- choice_probabilities(f$matrix, my_data)
ch
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>    item correct alternatives p         counts   
#>   <int> <chr>   <list>       <list>    <list>   
#> 1     1 dax     <chr [3]>    <dbl [3]> <dbl [3]>
#> 2     2 wug     <chr [3]>    <dbl [3]> <dbl [3]>
#> 3     3 fep     <chr [3]>    <dbl [3]> <dbl [3]>
# what the model predicts, and what people chose, for "wug"
wug <- rbind(model = ch$p[[2]], people = ch$counts[[2]] / sum(ch$counts[[2]]))
colnames(wug) <- ch$alternatives[[2]]
round(wug, 2)
#>         dax  wug  fep
#> model  0.25 0.63 0.12
#> people 0.30 0.50 0.20

See vignette("model-comparison") for fitting and comparing models by choice-level likelihood.
